name: Knee dislocation (multiligament knee injury)
populations: young adult males in high-energy trauma
summary: Disruption of two or more major knee ligaments, usually both cruciates, from high- or low-energy trauma. The knee may have spontaneously reduced; popliteal artery and peroneal nerve injury must be excluded.

keyFacts.label: Urgency
keyFacts.value: Emergency: limb-threatening popliteal artery injury in about 1 in 5

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ankle–brachial index: <0.90 detected all arterial injuries in one prospective series

keyFacts.label: Nerve injury
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about 25%

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Schenck anatomic (KD-I to KD-V, with C and N modifiers)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 12–18 months; return to any sport about 54%, high-level sport 22–33%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs, CT angiography if ABI <0.90 or abnormal pulses, then MRI

overview:
A knee dislocation is a complete loss of tibiofemoral contact. In practice the term covers any multiligament knee injury (MLKI) that disrupts both cruciates or one cruciate plus a collateral complex, because many dislocated knees reduce spontaneously before assessment and look deceptively normal [r1]. It is a limb-threatening emergency: across pooled studies, vascular injury occurred in 18% and nerve injury in 25%, and 12% of vascular injuries led to amputation [r2].

The immediate priorities are reduction, splinting and a documented neurovascular examination with an ankle–brachial index (ABI). An ABI below 0.90 identified every arterial injury requiring surgery in a prospective series [r4]. Most patients then undergo staged or single-stage ligament reconstruction; early surgery generally gives better outcomes than non-operative care or delayed surgery [r9,r10]. The physiotherapist leads a long, carefully protected rehabilitation that balances graft protection with the high risk of stiffness, while monitoring the peroneal nerve, which recovers in only about half of complete stretch injuries [r8,r11].

epidemiology.text: Knee dislocations are rare but likely under-recognised because many reduce before arrival. In a level I trauma centre series of 106 multiligament knees, the most common pattern (43%) was ACL plus PCL plus posterolateral corner; 25% had an ipsilateral tibial plateau fracture, 19% a femoral fracture, 25% a peroneal nerve injury, 21% an arterial injury and 16% compartment syndrome [r3]. Pooled data from 862 dislocations show vascular injury in 18% and nerve injury in 25%, with the highest vascular rates in KD-IIIL injuries (32%) and posterior dislocations (25%) [r2]. Ultra-low-velocity dislocations from minor falls in people with obesity are increasingly common and carry high neurovascular risk: in one series 27% had popliteal artery injury and 44% peroneal nerve injury [r6,r7].

intrinsic: Obesity (ultra-low-velocity dislocation from a simple fall or misstep) [r6,r7]
Previous multiligament injury or ligamentous laxity (expert opinion)
extrinsic: Motor vehicle and motorcycle crashes, pedestrian versus vehicle [r3]
High-speed contact and collision sports, skiing and motocross

mechanism.summary: Dislocation needs disruption of most of the knee's restraints. High-energy mechanisms (vehicle crashes, falls from height) and sports collisions apply hyperextension, a posterior force on the flexed tibia, or combined varus/valgus with rotation. Hyperextension tends to produce anterior dislocation: the posterior capsule and PCL fail and the popliteal artery, tethered above and below the knee, is stretched. A dashboard blow to the flexed knee produces posterior dislocation, which has a high vascular injury rate [r2]. In people with obesity, a low-energy fall or misstep can dislocate the knee [r6].
sequence: The foot is fixed and the knee near extension (sport) or flexed against a dashboard (vehicle).
A large force drives the knee into hyperextension, or drives the tibia backward, sometimes with varus or valgus and rotation.
The posterior capsule and the cruciate ligaments fail in quick succession; the collateral complexes follow depending on direction.
The tibia displaces completely relative to the femur (anterior, posterior, medial, lateral or rotatory).
The popliteal artery, tethered at the adductor hiatus and the soleal arch, is stretched or torn; intimal tears can thrombose hours later.
The common peroneal nerve is stretched around the fibular neck, especially with varus and posterolateral injury [r3].
The knee often reduces spontaneously as the limb is straightened, leaving gross multidirectional laxity and a deceptively normal shape [r1].

variants.name: Anterior (hyperextension) dislocation
variants.description: Forced hyperextension tears the posterior capsule and PCL, then the ACL; the popliteal artery is placed under traction.

variants.name: Posterior (dashboard) dislocation
variants.description: A posterior blow to the flexed proximal tibia, usually in a vehicle; associated with a high vascular injury rate [r2].

variants.name: Posterolateral (irreducible) dislocation
variants.description: The medial femoral condyle buttonholes through the medial capsule, leaving a skin 'dimple' over the medial joint line. It cannot be reduced closed and threatens the skin; it needs urgent open reduction (expert opinion).

variants.name: Ultra-low-velocity dislocation
variants.description: A simple fall or step in a person with obesity; neurovascular injury is common and reduction is often hard to maintain without external fixation [r6,r7].

anatomy.text: Knee stability depends on four ligament complexes: the ACL, the PCL, the medial complex (superficial and deep MCL, posterior oblique ligament) and the posterolateral corner (fibular collateral ligament, popliteus, popliteofibular ligament). A dislocation disrupts at least both cruciates or one cruciate and a collateral complex, and the Schenck anatomic classification describes which are torn [r1]. Behind the knee, the popliteal artery is fixed proximally at the adductor hiatus and distally at the fibrous arch of soleus, so it cannot move out of the way when the tibia displaces. The common peroneal nerve runs along the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the fibular neck, where varus and posterolateral injuries stretch it [r3].

structures.name: ACL and PCL
structures.role: Primary restraints to anterior and posterior tibial translation; both are torn in most dislocations [r1]

structures.name: Posterolateral corner
structures.role: Resists varus and external rotation; its injury is strongly linked to peroneal nerve injury [r3]

structures.name: Posterior capsule
structures.role: Resists hyperextension; tears in anterior (hyperextension) dislocations

structures.name: Popliteal artery
structures.role: Main blood supply to the leg below the knee, tethered above and below the joint and vulnerable to stretch, intimal tear and thrombosis [r2]

structures.name: Common peroneal nerve
structures.role: Supplies ankle dorsiflexors and evertors and sensation to the dorsum of the foot; stretched around the fibular neck [r8]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Dislocation tears multiple ligaments and the capsule over a large area, usually with bleeding into the joint and surrounding tissues. The popliteal artery may be transected, but more often it is stretched, producing an intimal flap that can thrombose over hours. This is why a normal pulse on arrival does not exclude arterial injury, and why serial examination for at least 48 hours has been advocated after KD-IV injuries [r5]. Warm ischaemia beyond a few hours causes irreversible muscle necrosis and amputation risk, and reperfusion after revascularisation can trigger compartment syndrome [r2,r3].

The common peroneal nerve suffers a traction injury that ranges from neuropraxia to a long zone of axonal disruption. Complete stretch injuries recovered spontaneously in about half of patients in one series, while transections did not recover without further surgery [r8]. Ligament healing then follows the usual inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, but the extensive capsular injury and the need for protection make arthrofibrosis a major risk, so rehabilitation must balance protection with early motion [r11].

structures.name: Cruciate ligaments
structures.effect: Usually both ruptured (KD-II to KD-IV); the ACL does not heal and the PCL heals poorly when grossly displaced [r1]

structures.name: Collateral complexes and posterolateral corner
structures.effect: Torn depending on direction of force; ACL + PCL + PLC was the most common pattern (43%) in one trauma series [r3]

structures.name: Popliteal artery
structures.effect: Intimal tear, thrombosis or transection in about 18%; 80% of these need repair [r2]

structures.name: Common peroneal nerve
structures.effect: Stretch injury or rupture in about 25%, especially with posterolateral injury [r2,r3]

structures.name: Bone
structures.effect: Associated tibial plateau (25%) or femoral (19%) fractures in high-energy injuries; fracture-dislocation is KD-V [r3]

structures.name: Menisci and articular cartilage
structures.effect: Frequently torn or contused, adding to long-term osteoarthritis risk

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Profound arthrogenic muscle inhibition and atrophy from effusion, pain and immobilisation [r13].

muscles.name: Ankle dorsiflexors and evertors
muscles.effect: Paralysed or weak if the peroneal nerve is injured, leading to foot drop and risk of equinus contracture [r8].

muscles.name: Leg compartments
muscles.effect: Ischaemia and reperfusion can cause compartment syndrome and muscle necrosis [r3].

cellular.description: Extensive bleeding into the joint and soft tissues; inflammatory cells infiltrate torn ligaments and capsule. Ischaemic muscle, if present, begins to die within hours.
Distal to an axonal injury, the axon and myelin break down and are cleared by Schwann cells and macrophages, preparing the path for regrowth.
Fibroblasts lay down scar in torn collateral structures and capsule; reconstructed grafts revascularise. Capsular scarring drives the risk of stiffness [r11].
Collagen and grafts mature slowly. Regenerating axons grow distally over months, so peroneal nerve recovery is judged over a long period [r8].

systems.effect: Popliteal artery injury threatens the limb; delayed thrombosis can occur after an initially normal examination [r2,r5].
Peroneal nerve palsy causes foot drop and sensory loss; quadriceps inhibition is profound [r8,r13].
High-energy cases carry intra-abdominal injury (13%), severe head injury (10%) and symptomatic pulmonary embolism (5%) [r3].
Long recovery, possible permanent foot drop and loss of work or sport affect mood; return to high-level sport is uncommon [r12].
Residual laxity, stiffness and meniscal and chondral damage increase the risk of osteoarthritis.

grading.system: Schenck anatomic classification of knee dislocation (Wascher modification)

grades.description: One cruciate torn with a collateral complex (e.g. ACL + PLC); a dislocation without bicruciate injury.
grades.prognosis: Best outcomes of the dislocation group

grades.description: Both cruciates torn; collateral complexes intact.
Both cruciates plus the medial (KD-IIIM) or lateral/posterolateral (KD-IIIL) complex. KD-IIIL had the highest pooled vascular injury rate (32%) [r2].
grades.prognosis: Reconstruction; posterolateral involvement increases peroneal nerve risk [r3]

grades.description: Both cruciates and both collateral complexes. Most flow-limiting arterial injuries in one series were KD-IV [r5].
grades.prognosis: Poorer return to unmodified work than lower grades [r12]

grades.description: Fracture-dislocation. Modifiers: C = arterial injury, N = nerve injury.
grades.prognosis: Depends on fracture and neurovascular injury; vascular injury lowers return to work [r12]

timeframes.summary: Recovery is long. After emergency care and reconstruction (often staged), protected rehabilitation lasts months and return to demanding activity typically takes 12–18 months. Many people need work modifications and few return to high-level sport [r12].

healing.description: Reduction, splinting, vascular assessment; bleeding and inflammation
Scar and graft incorporation; brace, protected weight-bearing, early controlled motion
Graft maturation and slow axonal regeneration

milestones.label: Ligament surgery (ideal window)
milestones.note: Early surgery (≤3 weeks) gave better outcomes than delayed surgery [r9]

timeframes.returnToSport: Return to any sport occurs in about 54% overall and about 59% after surgical treatment, but only 22–33% return to high-level sport [r12]. Return is rarely before 12 months and depends on stability, strength, nerve function and the patient's goals. These are typical ranges; progression is criteria-based.

symptoms: Severe pain and inability to bear weight after a high-energy injury, or after a simple fall in a person with obesity
The knee 'came out of place' and may have gone back in
Numbness or tingling in the foot; difficulty lifting the foot
A cold, pale or painful foot (vascular compromise)
Gross instability in every direction once pain allows movement
signs: Obvious deformity, or a knee that looks normal but is unstable in multiple planes (spontaneously reduced)
Absent, weak or asymmetrical dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses; ABI < 0.90
Popliteal swelling or haematoma; extensive bruising
Foot drop and reduced sensation on the dorsum of the foot
A skin dimple over the medial joint line (irreducible posterolateral dislocation)

subjective: Mechanism and energy: vehicle, motorcycle, fall from height, sport collision, or minor fall in a person with obesity
Was the knee deformed, and did it reduce by itself or by someone else?
Foot sensation, ability to move the foot, colour and temperature
Other injuries (head, chest, abdomen, other limbs) in high-energy trauma
Anticoagulant use and venous thromboembolism risk factors
observation: Deformity, skin integrity (open injury, dimple sign)
Colour and capillary refill of the foot
Position of rest: the knee may sag posteriorly or into varus/valgus
palpation: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses compared with the other side
rangeOfMotion: Do not force range in the emergency setting
After reconstruction: track extension and flexion weekly to catch early arthrofibrosis [r11]
strength: Ankle dorsiflexion, eversion and great-toe extension (peroneal nerve)
neuro: Common peroneal nerve: dorsiflexion, eversion, great-toe extension, first web space and dorsal foot sensation
Tibial nerve: plantarflexion, toe flexion, plantar sensation
Document findings before and after any reduction or splinting
functional: Later: gait, step-down, single-leg control and hop tests when cleared

specialTests.name: Ankle–brachial index (ABI)
specialTests.procedure: With a Doppler probe and cuff, measure systolic pressure at the ankle (dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial) on the injured side and divide by the brachial systolic pressure.
specialTests.positive: ABI < 0.90 indicates arterial injury and the need for vascular imaging and surgical review. In a prospective series, ABI < 0.90 had 100% sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value for arterial injury requiring surgery [r4].

specialTests.name: Serial pulse examination
specialTests.purpose: Detect delayed thrombosis from an intimal tear
specialTests.procedure: Palpate distal pulses and check capillary refill, colour and temperature repeatedly, comparing sides.
specialTests.positive: Any reduction or asymmetry in pulses or perfusion. Selective arteriography guided by physical examination was safe in a prospective series; serial examination for 48 hours is advised for KD-IV injuries [r5].

specialTests.name: Multiplanar laxity examination (once safe)
specialTests.purpose: Identify which ligament complexes are torn (Schenck class)
specialTests.procedure: Lachman, posterior drawer, varus and valgus stress at 0° and 30°, and dial test, usually under anaesthesia or once pain allows.
specialTests.positive: Laxity of both cruciates with or without one or both collateral complexes [r1].

clinicalRules.name: ABI-guided vascular imaging
clinicalRules.description: In knee dislocation, measure the ABI in every patient. ABI < 0.90 or abnormal pulses: urgent CT angiography and vascular surgery. ABI ≥ 0.90 with normal pulses: admit for serial examination [r4,r5].

outcomeMeasures.name: Lysholm score
outcomeMeasures.use: Symptoms and function; used in multiligament outcome reviews [r10]

outcomeMeasures.name: Tegner activity scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Activity level and return to work or sport [r12]

outcomeMeasures.name: Range of motion and stress radiographs
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective monitoring of stiffness and residual laxity

imaging.findings: Direction of dislocation, congruent reduction, associated fractures (KD-V), avulsions (Segond, fibular head)

imaging.indication: ABI < 0.90, abnormal pulses or hard signs of vascular injury
imaging.findings: Popliteal artery occlusion, intimal flap or transection [r4]

imaging.indication: Once the limb is safe, to map ligament, meniscal and cartilage injuries for surgical planning
imaging.findings: Cruciate, collateral and capsular tears; posterolateral corner injury; bone bruises

imaging.indication: Persisting peroneal nerve palsy at about 3 months
imaging.findings: Degree of axonal loss and early signs of reinnervation

differentials.name: Isolated PCL injury
differentials.distinguishing: Posterior laxity alone, with collaterals stable. Grade III posterior laxity (>10–12 mm) should prompt a search for combined injury.

differentials.name: Posterolateral corner injury
differentials.distinguishing: Varus and external rotation laxity; may be part of a KD-I or KD-IIIL injury.

differentials.name: Tibial plateau fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness and fracture on radiographs. High-energy plateau fractures can be fracture-dislocations (KD-V) with the same neurovascular risks.

differentials.name: Lateral patellar dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Often confused by patients ('my knee dislocated'). The patella displaces laterally, the tibiofemoral joint is stable and neurovascular injury is rare.

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Can coexist after high-energy injury or revascularisation; pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment.

differentials.name: Tibial and fibular shaft fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Deformity is below the joint and radiographs show the fracture; check the knee for associated ligament injury.

redFlags: Hard signs of arterial injury (absent pulses, cold pale foot, expanding or pulsatile popliteal haematoma, bruit or thrill): immediate emergency and vascular surgery referral; delays beyond a few hours risk amputation [r2].
ABI below 0.90, or pulses that weaken over the first 48 hours: urgent CT angiography and vascular review [r4,r5].
Severe pain out of proportion, a tense leg and pain on passive toe stretch, especially after revascularisation: suspect compartment syndrome and arrange emergency fasciotomy assessment [r3].
A skin dimple over the medial joint line or a dislocation that will not reduce: urgent orthopaedic review for open reduction to protect the skin.
New or worsening foot drop or numbness: document and refer urgently [r8].
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness during recovery: suspect DVT or pulmonary embolism (symptomatic PE in 5% of one trauma series) [r3].

management.principles: Emergency management comes first: reduce the knee, splint it, and document a full neurovascular examination with an ABI. ABI < 0.90 or abnormal pulses requires urgent vascular imaging and repair; otherwise the patient is observed with serial examinations [r4,r5]. Ligament management is individualised, but surgical treatment gives better function, return to work and return to sport than non-operative care, and surgery within about 3 weeks gives better outcomes than delayed surgery [r9,r10]. Reconstruction is preferred to repair, especially for the posterolateral corner [r9]. An external fixator is used when reduction cannot be maintained, with vascular repair, or in ultra-low-velocity dislocations in people with obesity [r7]. Rehabilitation protects the reconstructed structures in a hierarchy, with emerging evidence that many patients are over-protected, at the cost of stiffness [r11].

medical.name: Urgent reduction, splinting and vascular assessment
medical.description: Closed reduction as soon as possible, splinting in slight flexion, ABI in all patients and CT angiography for ABI < 0.90 or abnormal pulses [r4].

medical.name: Vascular repair and fasciotomy
medical.description: Popliteal artery repair or bypass for arterial injury (about 80% of vascular injuries are repaired), with prophylactic fasciotomy often performed after revascularisation [r2].

medical.name: Multiligament reconstruction (single-stage or staged)
medical.description: Surgical reconstruction gives better outcomes than non-operative care; early surgery (≤3 weeks) is generally better than delayed surgery, and reconstruction is more reliable than repair [r9,r10].

medical.name: External fixation
medical.description: Temporary spanning external fixator when reduction cannot be held, after vascular repair, with open injuries, or in patients with severe obesity [r7].

medical.name: Non-operative treatment (brace or cast)
medical.description: Associated with lower rates of excellent/good outcomes and return to work and sport than surgery in active patients; reserved for patients unfit for surgery or with low demands [r9].

medical.name: VTE prophylaxis
medical.description: Pharmacological and mechanical prophylaxis per trauma protocol given immobilisation and high-energy injury [r3].

physio.name: Structured, protected post-operative rehabilitation
physio.description: Phase-based program guided by which structures need most protection (e.g. PCL and posterolateral reconstructions), with early quadriceps activation and controlled range of motion [r11].

physio.name: Early controlled range of motion to prevent arthrofibrosis
physio.description: Prone or supported passive range of motion from early after surgery within surgeon limits; close monitoring of extension and flexion. Excessive protection may contribute to stiffness [r11].

physio.name: Peroneal palsy management
physio.description: Ankle–foot orthosis, daily dorsiflexion stretching to prevent equinus, and serial nerve examination; tendon transfer may later be considered if no recovery [r8].

physio.name: Prolonged rigid immobilisation without motion
physio.description: Increases the risk of stiffness and quadriceps atrophy without clear stability benefit (expert opinion).

physio.name: Graded return to work and sport
physio.description: Many patients return to work, often with modifications; return to high-level sport is uncommon, so set goals early and realistically [r12].

education: A dislocated knee can damage the main artery behind the knee, so blood flow is checked carefully and repeatedly at first.
Most people need surgery to rebuild several ligaments, usually within the first few weeks.
Recovery takes at least a year. Early movement within safe limits matters because stiffness is a common problem.
If the nerve to the foot was stretched, recovery is slow and can take months; a foot splint helps you walk safely meanwhile.
Report a cold, pale or painful foot, increasing calf tightness, or breathlessness immediately.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation follows reconstruction and is guided by the surgeon's protocol and the hierarchy of structures needing protection (PCL and posterolateral or medial reconstructions usually take priority over the ACL) [r11]. Typical early restrictions include a hinged brace, protected weight-bearing for about 6 weeks, prone or supported range of motion to avoid posterior tibial sag, and no resisted hamstring work. Progress on criteria (quiet knee, range, quadriceps control, stable laxity), and watch closely for arthrofibrosis and nerve or vascular complications.

stages.name: Protect, activate & move
goals: Full passive extension and progressive flexion to ~90°
Manage oedema, pain and foot drop
precautions: Brace and weight-bearing per surgeon (often touch-weight-bearing for 6 weeks)
Support the proximal tibia to prevent posterior sag; prone flexion
No varus/valgus stress or resisted hamstring work
Monitor pulses, compartments, wounds, calf (DVT) and nerve function

exercises.name: Prone passive knee flexion
exercises.cues: Strap or therapist lifts the shin

exercises.name: Ankle pumps and calf/dorsiflexion stretch
exercises.cues: Prevents equinus with a peroneal palsy

progressionCriteria: Wounds healed and limb neurovascularly stable

stages.name: Restore range, gait & strength
precautions: Closed-chain work in a limited arc (about 0–60°) to protect the PCL
Flag flexion < 90° at 8–12 weeks for surgeon review (arthrofibrosis)
progressionCriteria: No increase in laxity on examination

stages.name: Strength & control
goals: Progressive strength of quadriceps, hip and (gradually) hamstrings
Begin running toward month 6 if criteria met

stages.name: Function, work & sport
goals: Return to work with or without modifications
precautions: Return to pivoting or contact sport only after surgeon review, typically ≥ 12 months
Set realistic goals: high-level sport return is uncommon [r12]

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Every second day, building to 20–30 min

progressionCriteria: Strength and hop LSI ≥ 85–90% for sport
Safe gait and orthotic strategy if peroneal palsy persists

criteria: At least 9–12 months after reconstruction and surgeon clearance
Full or functional range of motion without effusion
Quadriceps and hamstring strength ≥ 90% of the other side
Adequate dorsiflexion strength, or a safe orthotic solution
tests: IKDC Subjective Knee Form and Tegner scale

prognosis: Function after multiligament knee injury is usually good enough for daily life and most work, but rarely normal. In a systematic review of 524 patients, 53.6% returned to any sport (59.1% in surgically treated cohorts), 22–33% to high-level sport, 88.4% to any work and 62.1% to work with little or no modification; obesity, non-operative treatment, higher Schenck grade and vascular injury predicted poorer outcomes [r12]. Vascular injury carried a 12% amputation rate in pooled data [r2]. About half of complete peroneal nerve stretch injuries recover spontaneously; the rest need an orthosis or tendon transfer [r8]. Stiffness, residual laxity and post-traumatic osteoarthritis are common long-term problems.
prevention: Road safety measures (seat belts, motorcycle protective equipment) reduce high-energy knee trauma (general advice; no knee-specific trials).
Weight management may reduce the risk of ultra-low-velocity dislocation in people with severe obesity (expert opinion).
clinicalPearls: A knee with gross laxity in more than one plane is a dislocated knee until proven otherwise, even if it looks normal [r1].
A palpable pulse does not exclude arterial injury. Measure the ABI in every case and repeat the vascular examination [r4,r5].
Consider dislocation in a person with obesity who 'just fell' and cannot weight-bear; neurovascular injury is common in these low-energy injuries [r6].
Posterolateral injury and peroneal palsy travel together. Check the nerve before and after every intervention [r3].
Stiffness is the enemy after reconstruction. Measure range at every visit and escalate early if progress stalls [r11].
Set expectations early: most people return to work, but few return to high-level sport [r12].

forces.label: Tibia driven forward off the femur

captions.text: A rugby player carries the ball with the right foot planted and the knee straight.
A defender drives low into the front of the knee.
The knee is forced into severe hyperextension against the fixed foot.
The posterior capsule and both cruciates fail and the tibia dislocates forward.
The knee may slip back into place, looking normal while the leg's blood supply is at risk.
Zooming into the right knee from the side; the popliteal artery runs behind the joint.
Viewed from the side: the PCL lies behind the ACL, and the posterior capsule closes the joint behind.
Hyperextension tears the posterior capsule first, then the cruciate ligaments.
With both cruciates gone, the tibia dislocates forward in front of the femur.
The popliteal artery, tethered above and below the knee, is stretched and may tear or clot.
Bleeding fills the joint and soft tissues; the capsule tear lets fluid escape into the calf.
The knee often relocates by itself, hiding how severe the injury is.
Check pulses and measure the ankle–brachial index in every case, and repeat the checks.
The common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck, close to the posterolateral knee.
Traction stretches the nerve and its small blood vessels, starving it of oxygen.
Milder stretch damages the myelin sheath only: conduction blocks but axons survive.
Greater stretch tears axons over a long segment of nerve.
Below the tear, axons and myelin break down and macrophages clear the debris.
Axons regrow slowly over months; about half of complete stretch injuries recover.
